en: The Dharma Gate of the Recitation Method for the Lotus Family Yoga of the Accomplishment of the Great Compassion of Avalokiteśvara, in one fascicle.
Compiled by the Grand Master of the Court, Peer of the State, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Sui.

The Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Monastery—honored with a purple robe, granted a fief of three thousand households, posthumously bestowed the title of Minister of Works, and given the epithet Dajian (Great Mirror)—translated this by imperial decree. For all those who wish to practice within this gateway:
One must know the sequence of ritual procedures;
if one does not fully understand the liturgical manuals,
one's efforts will be in vain and time will be wasted.
Based on this, I have collated and synthesized the various events, dharmas, dharma-gates,
and yoga-gates found throughout the sūtras into a single work for the sake of those beginners seeking liberation.
Because they have attained the stages and positions,
I have compiled and perfected those practices for all who are training.
First, one should enter the Great Samaya Mandala of Empowerment,
receive the bodhisattva precepts and practices, give rise to the mind of great compassion,
and benefit sentient beings by relinquishing body, life, and wealth.
With single-minded devotion, one aspires toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
the body is free from attachment and aversion;
and with diligent, courageous resolve, one gathers the mind so that it is not distracted.
His loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity never ceased for even a moment,
enabling immeasurable sentient beings to cross to the other shore;
both internally and externally pure, he was rendered utterly majestic and pristine.
One should always show respect toward elders, preceptors, and ācāryas;
one’s mind should not be deceitful or crooked, and one’s speech must be truthful.
When a beggar comes, one should distribute alms accordingly;
one should not dismiss them empty-handed while engaged in the four postures or attending to various affairs.
In this manner, one should maintain clarity of mindfulness at every moment and at every interval.
Contemplate thoroughly that all conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent;
to speak briefly, all dharmas are like reflections in a mirror.
Having understood this, [one should practice].
One must don the armor of diligence,
take up the sword of secret mantras to destroy the army of afflictions, and shatter the fetters of the hindrances.
Having emerged from the delusory ocean of birth and death,
one reaches the site of enlightenment and sits upon the vajra-seat;
one must resolutely form this mind and not allow it to regress.
Only such persons as these should practice;
within this Mahāyāna realm, they give rise to the most excellent Dharma-gate.
Therefore, I shall now explain it in successive order.
For those who wish to perform recitation,
they must first purify the ground.
Regarding the method for purifying the ground, the area may be four cubits, eight cubits, twelve cubits, sixteen cubits, or similar dimensions.
Within these measurements, take as much as one’s strength allows.
Dig a depth of at least a knee or one cubit (*hasta*),
and clear away insects, ants, various shards and rubble, hair, ashes, charcoal, chaff, husks, thorns, tree roots, and all other such impure and foul substances.
Having filled the pure land, firmly packed it, and leveled it,
one should subsequently erect a vihāra upon it.
One should first determine the cardinal directions for the chamber and apply a clean coating to its interior.
If one seeks to eliminate calamities,
the room should have its door opening to the south,
and one should sit facing north.
At that time, one should sit with the two shins crossed.
If performing a rite for increase and prosperity, one should open the western gate and sit facing east in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
If one performs the rite of wrathful subjugation,
one should open the northern gate and sit facing south in a squatting posture.
Simply place the left foot over the right with both feet together.
If one is performing a rite for friendship and mutual affection,
one should open the eastern gate and sit facing west.
When sitting, one should sit with both legs extended and the two knees opened wide;
this is called the method for constructing a vihāra and the sitting posture for seeking success.
The ritual of the mudrā is thus.
First, prepare a pure chamber, or an open space,
or atop a rocky mountain or similar location, and construct the altar there. Then,
according to the specific objective one seeks, sit upon it following the aforementioned method of seating.
Once this hall has been constructed, it should first be smeared with cow dung according to the ritual rules.
At that time, one must first consecrate it with mantras before using it.
When first sweeping the floor, one should recite this mantra, which says:
Oṃ hāra hāra raurukāra haraṇaya svāhā. Recite this mantra three times while sweeping the ground.
Having finished sweeping the ground, when one wishes to clear away the sweepings, one should again recite this mantra, saying:
Oṃ śuddhe mahāśuddhe kṣānti svāhā. Reciting this mantra three times, one should remove the soil.
Having removed the earth, smear the altar with cow dung.
Recite this mantra: Oṃ karale mahākarale svāhā. Having recited this mantra, use it for the purpose of smearing and adorning.
When washing the various offering vessels and the vessels for scented water, one should employ this mantra, which is recited as follows:

*Namo siddhye svāhā* (Namo siddhye). *Sarvatathāgatebhyo oṃ veraveri mahāpācale sadasata sarati sarati dāridari vidhamani sambhañjani tarumati siddhakarī tṛpya svāhā.* Recite this mantra three times while washing all the offering implements.
The reason for reciting this mantra is to purify and eliminate all transgressions and defilements resulting from violations of the *samaya* precepts.
As for the articles of offering:
Before making offerings, place them all together in a clean location.
Recite this vidyā-mantra and perform this mudrā; the mantra is:
Oṃ śikhari vajri. As for the characteristics of this mantra-mudrā:
One should form it by grasping the thumb with the three fingers from the middle finger downward of the right hand, making the thumb the peak,
and then extending the index finger straight upward; thus it is accomplished.
Seal the objects with this mudrā and brandish it clockwise to protect all incense,
flowers, lamps, food, drink, and so forth.
Thereafter, proceed to the bathing place.
When performing this rite, it may be done either by oneself or by having a disciple perform it; both ways are acceptable.
When one wishes to bind the mudrā:
Having first bound the seals of the three samādhis,
one may then proceed to bind the seals.
As for the characteristics of these samādhis:
First, the Samaya-mudrā of the Buddha Family: First, place both hands side by side.
Join the middle fingers together as when normally holding an object.
Then, touch the tips of the index fingers to the upper joints of the respective middle fingers.
Next, press the tips of the index fingers with the two thumbs; this is the mudrā.
The mantra for this mudrā is:
Oṃ tathāgatapūjāye svāhā. Recite this mantra and place this mudrā upon the crown of the head.
One should contemplate that this seal is identical to the true body of the Tathāgata, being without any difference;
whoever beholds this seal beholds the Buddha.
Next, the Samaya Seal of the Lotus Family is explained.
With the palms of both hands joined at their bases,
extend the two hands with the ten fingers splayed apart,
and place the two thumbs side by side with their tips touching.
Again, do the same with the two little fingers;
thus the mudrā is formed.
Then, raise it and place it upon the head, as if near the right side.
One should form this visualization: this mudrā is the Noble Sovereign Mantra of the Bodhisattva, which is:
Oṃ padmamabhāṣaya svāhā. Next, the Samaya-mudrā of the Vajra Family is explained.
One should place the backs of the two hands together,
with the right hand pressing down on the left and the fingers interlaced in reverse order;
thereafter, one should cross the right little finger over the left thumb.
Furthermore, cross the right thumb over the left little finger.
This is the mudrā and mantra, which is recited as follows:
Oṃ vajra-pavaye svāhā. With this mudrā, raise it above the head, keeping it near the left side.
Visualize that this mudrā is the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
Having performed this triple samaya-mudrā,
one may then proceed to bind all other mudrās.
For those who follow these secret treasury mantras,
I shall now explain their essentials according to this sequence for all practitioners.
At the first break of dawn, before undertaking any activity, one who intends to go out or enter should first form the mudrā and recite the vidyā-mantra; only after this should they rise to act.
This vidyā-mantra is as follows:
Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo vajrapāṇaye mahāyakṣasenāpataye. Namo vajrakrodhāya daṃṣṭrākarālāya.
Tadyathā | Oṃ | Amṛta-kuṇḍali | Kha kha khāhi khāhi | Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha | Bandha bandha | Hana hana | Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa | Bhīṣaya bhīṣaya | Sā... || 14 || Sa || 15 ||
BAVIJÑĀNA-VIÑCAYA-GAŅAPATI-VITANDAKARĀYA (15) HŪṂ PHAṬ (16) SVĀHĀ.
As for the mudrā of this mantra, one should use both hands.
Place the thumbs upon the nails of the little fingers respectively.
Having extended the remaining three fingers,
cross the arms so that the right presses against the left.
Each is formed as a seal upon the shoulders.
Within the mind, one should form this image:
the two feet stand in the shape of the character "八" (eight).
Puffing out his cheeks and biting his right lip,
he assumes a wrathful expression and recites the mantra seven times.
If one wishes to bind obstructive spirits and other such beings, [one should do so].
Then, form fists with both hands and bind the three fingers;
while binding them, one should say: "Bandha bandha."
Having performed these rites, one may then leave the room.
If one wishes to enter places that are defiled by contact,
or to go to the latrine and so forth, one must likewise protect oneself.
As for this mudrā: with the two little fingers and the two ring fingers of both hands, cross them inwardly with the right hand pressing over the left;
the two middle fingers are held upright with their tips touching one another.
Place the two index fingers upon the upper joints of the two middle fingers,
leaving a space of about one-tenth of an inch between them on their backs;
then extend both thumbs upright.
Grasp the middle fingers together;
this constitutes the *rakṣā-mudrā*. The mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-jñi-pratyan-taya svāhā. Using this mudrā, seal the five places.
The five locations are: the top of the head, the two shoulders, the heart, and the throat.
These are called the five locations.
This is known as the method for protecting the body; when going to the latrine, one should snap one's fingers three times.
Having become alert, one performs the finger-snapping ritual upon it, reciting the mantra:
*Oṃ kili kili rāva-lodara hūṃ phaṭ*. Recite once for each finger snap, up to three times.
When washing the hands, one should visualize the mantra and form of Cundī in the mind, and then wash the hands.
Having washed the hands, one rinses the mouth; for the rinsing-mouth mudrā, bend the middle and ring fingers of the right hand into the palm.
Extend the thumb, index finger, and little finger straight to receive the water, and rinse three times with this mantra:
*Oṃ cūcūle kuru kuru svāhā*. Having used this mudrā and mantra to rinse one's mouth, thereafter—
Regarding the mudrā for purifying the body and removing obstructing spirits, ghosts, and deities who conceal their forms:
form fists with both hands,
then extend the index fingers of each hand.
Insert the tip of the right index finger into the left fist and grasp it;
likewise, insert the tip of the left index finger into the right fist. The mantra is as follows:
Recite "Oṃ hana hana amṛte hūṃ pe" three times.
Gently stroke [the body] starting from the head and proceeding downward, performing this three times.
This will cause all demonic obstacles within the body to be completely extinguished.
One should visualize that all the demons have departed,
and subsequently perform the seal for binding all demons.
One should beckon him outward with the left hand. Then,
one should turn the back of the right hand over onto the back of the left hand,
and having interlaced all eight fingers, [one should perform the mudrā].
Then, turn it to the left;
flipping it toward the heart, form a fist with both hands and place them upon the heart with both thumbs extended upright.
Then, placing the right elbow inside the left elbow,
draw it outward; having thus placed the mudrā upon the head, [proceed].
Then, opening that seal and slowly lowering it, one recites the mantra as follows:
Oṃ kili kili bilādra prakarṣi mahāghurute jayane ghaṭa hūṃ phaṭ paṃta paṃta svāhā. By the power of this seal and mantra, [the following occurs].
This enables all Māras and their like to be bound.
Then, visualize yourself clad in adamantine armor.
Having performed this rite:
When performing ablutions, one should follow the ritual procedures for bathing according to the *dhāraṇī-vinaya* and the *siddhi* texts;
it should be understood that if one uses only the minor *dhāraṇī* of Cundā, [the following applies].
When using this for one's own bathing or self-consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one may also recite the mantra:
*Oṃ amṛte hūṃ pe*. As for the mudrā of the three families:
with the right hand, press the thumb upon the nail of the little finger.
The other three fingers are simply extended straight;
with this mudrā and mantra, one sprinkles oneself and one's robes,
and consecrates the water for bathing, putting on clothes, and so forth.
It may be used for both [purposes].
When bathing, one should single-mindedly recollect the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others,
ensuring that the mind does not become distracted.
Visualize that the deity and oneself are non-different, and perform the ablution.
First, visualize the deity, the Three Jewels, and so forth as if they were present before one's eyes.
Then, offer three handfuls of the bathing water.
For this mudrā, one should form the hollowed cup with both hands as usual;
however, one simply joins the tips of the two thumbs and the two index fingers together.
First offer it to the Buddha, and the mantra is recited three times.
Oṃ tīre tīre buddhāya svāhā. Next, offer the mantra for the Dharma three times: Oṃ tīre tīre dharmāya svāhā.
Next, offer the mantra for the Saṅgha, reciting it three times: [Oṃ tīre tīre saṅghāya svāhā].
Oṃ dṛte dṛte saṃghāya svāhā. Next, when offering water to the *iṣṭadevatā* (the tutelary deity), recite the general mantra for the three [offerings] as follows:
Oṃ arghaṃ bhagavan pratīccha imaṃ svāhā. When offering the water to the *iṣṭadevatā*, [recite this].
Alternatively, one may also recite the original mantra.
Having performed this rite according to one's ability within the river waters where one has bathed,
and having brought the original mantra to mind, [one should proceed].
He slowly emerges.
When taking up his robes to wear them, he recites this mantra.
He sprinkles water upon the robes and then takes them up to put them on, with the following incantation:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānamūrti svāhā. Having sprinkled water with this, when one is about to put on the robes, one should recite this mantra three times.
"Oṃ vaimalyapariśuddhavajri hūṃ. This mantra-seal is simply formed by making a fist with each of the two hands.
When putting on any clothing, necklaces, crowns, bracelets, armlets, or any other ornaments for the body, one should recite this mantra.
When performing these rites, one should not give rise to anger.
Furthermore, one should not look upon anything that is evil, foul, or inauspicious.
Once the ritual bathing is completed, one proceeds toward the vihāra.
One should not go barefoot;
one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus flower beneath one's feet to support them,
and one's body should be identical in form to that of the deity.
On both sides, the eight classes of devas and nagas were fully present,
surrounding and attending him from front and rear as his retinue.
Furthermore, he visualized the Honored One before him, appearing with solemn clarity.
One should not ride upon the grasses, trees,
or shrubs growing along the path, nor upon any images, down to those in the form of animals, while crossing over them.
One must not step upon any articles of offering, nor the reflections of stupas, images, or the shadows of masters and monks.
Upon reaching the precincts of the vihāra,
one must further wash and purify oneself according to the Dharma before entering.
When first about to enter,
one should utter the sound "HŪṂ" as the door is being opened and then enter.
Once inside the chamber before the Buddha, one should form this mental resolve:
The true bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the great Dharma Kings of the three periods of time, abide eternally;
my fleshly eyes do not personally perceive or see them.
I pray that you may behold me with your path-eye as I take refuge.
Having formed this thought, one should prostrate with the three karmas and the five limbs, reverently and solemnly offering salutation.
One should also speak these words: "I now pay respectful homage.
Having completed the salutation, one should, as usual, perform repentance, rejoice in merit, and extensively make great vows.
Vowing to cultivate goodness and so forth, he immediately burned incense.
By means of this fragrance, he then eliminated all malevolent spirits and ghosts; the incense mantra was as follows:
From this point forward, it is used for all the rites of the Vajradhātu and other families.
Recite: Oṃ padmāni mahāye mahāye jaye mahāni svāhā. Having performed this rite, [proceed].
Furthermore, recite the mantra over water and scatter it in the four directions to form a protective boundary.
The mantra for this rite is: Oṃ aruḥ svāhā. Having completed this rite, [proceed].
Furthermore, perform the method of visualization:
first visualize the syllable *hrīḥ*.
From this syllable, Amitāyus Tathāgata arises, his physical form complete and perfect.
From the body of the Tathāgata flows forth a wondrously fragrant milk-water,
which forms a great ocean.
Within this ocean, one should visualize the syllable *praṃ*, which transforms into a tortoise.
Its dimensions are immeasurable yojanas in length and breadth,
and its color is like that of gold.
One should visualize a lotus flower upon the tortoise.
The flower has eight petals,
each with three layers.
One should visualize this flower as arising from the syllable HṚĪḤ.
Then, within the flower, one visualizes the syllable *su*.
On both sides of this syllable, one visualizes a *hūṃ* syllable.
All these syllables together form a single Mount Sumeru.
The mountain has eight peaks composed of various jewels.
Within this mountain, one further observes five chambers;
these chambers appear to be five externally, yet are of a single uniform aspect internally.
Within this chamber, one should visualize eight great vajra pillars,
composed of exquisite jewels interspersed with inlaid gems of rare beauty and brilliant adornment;
above them are makara heads fashioned of jade, from which hang jeweled chains.
Golden bells were suspended from it, with necklaces and jeweled curtains hanging all around;
the precious canopy was adorned with *bodhi*-flowers,
while tassels, nets, and sashes hung down in profusion, interlacing one another.
The ground is composed of precious substances such as crystal, where pure light reflects one another;
upon it are strewn famous flowers such as the *kusuma*,
and the fragrance of pure-precept ointments is exceptionally rich and sublime.
The fragrance of burning incense wafts forth as they ascend in liberation;
the light of the wisdom-maṇi lamps shines with brilliant radiance;
rows of jewel trees stand in formation, and as a gentle fragrant breeze touches them, their blossoms all burst forth in perfume.
Variegated silk banners fluttered in profusion, interspersed with precious platters and alternating with jeweled vases;
there were also various and immeasurable numbers of yakṣas, rākṣasas, devas, and other such beings.
Surrounded by attendants before and behind, they performed various musical instruments,
danced the Vajra dance, and sang songs of praise to the Vajra;
auspicious clouds spread everywhere.
From within the clouds, immeasurable supramundane incense and flowers rained down,
filling the void as they fell slowly and in profusion;
various fragrant foods and perfumed drinks were interlaced throughout.
One should install it and make offerings.
A practitioner of the Dharma should thus contemplate with clarity and stability,
until it accords with the mind as vividly as if it were distinct and bright.
When entering this contemplation, one should recite this mantra; it is applicable to all three families (*trikula*), as is the aforementioned visualization, though there are slight differences.
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānām*. *Tadyathā*: *Ucchritatejasi spharaṇi gaganaspharaṇi svāhā*. By reciting this vidyā-mantra, one enters into the various samādhis.
Whatever one contemplates according to one's mind will all be accomplished;
these are the true words of the Buddha and should not be regarded as false.
The reason for first performing this contemplation is the desire to become free from internal and external objects of focus, thereby attaining purity.
Just as space is unattached to anything, one should likewise purify the body.
Furthermore, recite this mantra together with the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*). The mantra is as follows; this vidyā is employed for the three families.
Oṃ sarvabījodhāra sarvadharma svabhāvaviśuddha. Having recited this mantra, one purifies one's own body.
He further spoke these words:
"For immeasurable kalpas, we have wandered through the cycle of birth and death,
submerged in the mud of afflictions and never having encountered a virtuous friend."
Yet, following after deluded thoughts, they are unable to achieve liberation and do not give rise to aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way;
therefore, may I cause them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
One should vocally recite the letter A.
The reason for reciting this letter is that the letter A signifies the meaning of non-arising.
This leads to the gate of emptiness and stillness.
Only this gate can distance one from dust and defilement;
those who accord with this Dharma can eliminate the sins of a practitioner numbering as many as motes of dust accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
It is like the bright sun shining universally across the pure sky;
all darkness naturally disperses and becomes clear.
The "sun" is the sun of wisdom, and the "sky" is the sky of the mantra.
With this sun of wisdom, one illuminates the void of incantations and the darkness of deep afflictions;
with a clear and pure mind, one contemplates the realm of space.
Pervading throughout that space are forms of Tathāgatas,
as large as sesame seeds and complete with all the primary and secondary marks;
all these Tathāgatas stand before the practitioner.
Tapping his fingers to rouse [the practitioner], he said to him:
"Good son, if you wish to give rise to the bodhicitta,
you should observe your own mind."
At that time, having received these words,
the practitioner should leap for joy and rise from their seat.
Before each of the Tathāgatas, they should prostrate themselves with all five limbs on the ground and pay homage with single-minded devotion.
When making offerings to the Buddhas, one should recite this mantra, which is applicable to all three families (*trikula*).
It is as follows: *Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāpraṇāmakara mi*. Having recited this mantra, one should visualize that one has paid homage to all the Tathāgatas.
One should immediately observe one's own mind.
When observing one's own mind, one should recite this mantra, which says:
Oṃ citta-prativedha-kara mi. One should recite this vidyā-mantra.
Within his own mind, he beheld a single moon;
its shape was round and white, though not yet entirely distinct.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying, "I have already seen the mind."
"It is like the moon that has not yet become clear.
The Buddha said, "Good son, excellent, excellent! You have already seen the mind.
You should recite this vidyā-mantra and contemplate the mind again and again."
The mantra for making it extremely bright and pure is:
Oṃ bodhicitta-utpādayāmi. Having recited this vidyā-mantra and visualized the moon of the mind until it is utterly purified, [one should proceed].
Furthermore, for the sake of making the bodhicitta firm,
one should visualize a vajra-lotus atop that moon.
While visualizing this flower, one should recite this vidyā-mantra, which says:
Oṃ tiṣṭha vajrapadma. Reciting this vidyā-mantra, one should visualize it upon the flower; atop that flower, there is a vajra.
Because it possesses these characteristics, it is called the Vajra Lotus.
One should form this thought:
"This mind of mine is not different from the Vajra Lotus."
Gradually blossoming, its light becomes blazing and fills all things inexhaustibly.
At the time of entering this Vajra Lotus Blossom Samādhi,
one further recites this mantra:
Oṃ sphaḥ ra ba dha ma. Reciting this vidyā-mantra, one contemplates these flowers.
The radiance of the flowers illuminates the wondrous lands of immeasurable buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thereupon, within that light, there emerged a vast array of lotus-manifestations.
From within these lotus-sections, according to what each practitioner upholds, there arose the voices of celestial beings— pure, moist, and resonant—
as they humbly petitioned the Tathāgatas of all such lands.
They enter into these flowers.
Once all these Tathāgatas have entered these flowers,
they then gradually contract these wondrous blossoms.
It remains as it was before, without change;
according to one's capacity, one can manifest this body in various sizes and abide therein.
This is when one performs the Sword-Flower Samādhi.
One should recite this mantra, saying:
Oṃ saṃhara vajrapadma. Having recited this vidyā-mantra, one should gather the flowers and remain there according to their size.
Furthermore, one enters the body of the Vajra-Lotus.
This Lotus of Samaya-Vajra constitutes my own body.
When entering this visualization, one should again recite this mantra.
Oṃ vajrapadma-kūṇca samayakūṇca mahāsamayakūṇca. Having thus visualized this vajra-lotus body, one should immediately visualize one's own body as being identical in form to that deity.
The reason for entering the visualization of Avalokiteśvara first is that one desires to firmly and swiftly manifest the vajra-body,
and further vows that in every successive birth one shall necessarily attain the body of a holy being.
Regarding the mantra and mudrā for entering contemplation:
one should interlace the three fingers below the index fingers of both hands with the palms facing outward.
Join the tips of the two index fingers together like lotus petals, extend and erect the two thumbs, and recite the mantra:
Oṃ hrīḥ sarvakarādiṣṭha svāhā hrīḥ. This seal and mantra are used in conjunction with the previous three families. Seal the four locations with this seal and mantra.
The heart, the space between the eyebrows, the throat, and the crown of the head—
these are the four places for the mantra.
Next, perform the rite of self-consecration.
This seal-sign enables the practitioner to swiftly attain the body of samādhi and achieve its full perfection.
This is the seal-sign.
Having joined the two hands in the usual manner of *añjali*,
one should then contract the four fingers below the index finger,
pressing their tips against the backs of those fingers as they are laid flat.
To form the shape of a precious lotus, the mantra is recited as:
Oṃ dharmanī padma abhiṣeka hūṃ hrīḥ. Reciting this mantra, one raises the mudrā and places it upon the forehead.
It then disperses and parts, circling around the head;
having reached the crown of the head,
it descends slowly along the body.
Finally, the mind abides upon the mind. Then,
forming vajra fists with both hands,
extend the thumbs and index fingers straight upward.
Visualize the syllable Oṃ on the face of the right index finger and the syllable Aḥ on the left index finger; then,
with both hands encircling the body, perform the rite of donning armor.
Having performed this rite,
all devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans,
and others shall see the practitioner as having a vajra body.
Clad in adamantine armor,
all demons, heretics, and the like dare not gaze upon it directly;
they retreat and flee in haste, unable to cause harm.
Having performed this rite,
one next contemplates the image of the primary deity before oneself,
visualizing it with its own form and the usual marks and signs of excellence.
Furthermore, as previously described,
one visualizes the five jewels of Mount Sumeru within the chamber,
specifically inside that inner chamber.
With single-minded concentration, clearly contemplate the Tathāgata Amitāyus,
who is endowed with all the primary and secondary marks and whose radiance is blazing and magnificent.
To the right of the Buddha is the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
On the left is Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva;
if there are other bodhisattvas from the same family,
they should be placed here.
Moving slightly forward to the right side,
as described in the original ritual manual,
all the celestial messengers [should be visualized].
And all the bodhisattvas and others are each established according to their inclinations.
Having performed this contemplation, [one should proceed].
One should then employ the syllables of the mantra one holds,
visualizing them being arranged one by one from the head down to the feet;
this should also be done according to the principles and skillful means of its specific meaning.
Having completed the visualization of the arrangement of syllables,
one immediately forms the *ratnacakravāhana-mudrā* (the seal of the precious chariot) to welcome the Noble One.
That which was previously visualized is called the mark of the *dharmakāya*.
That which is now being requested is called the "Body of Wisdom.
We entreat that Body of Wisdom to come and join with this Dharma-body.
For this reason, one first contemplates and subsequently makes the request.
As for this mudrā: first, with both hands held palm-upward, interlace the fingers inwardly;
place the tips of the two index fingers side by side against each other, and direct the two thumbs inward.
Pushing back the tips of the middle fingers,
this is called the Seal of the Precious Chariot (*ratnasyandana-mudrā*).
Visualize this precious chariot mounted upon five-colored clouds.
Go to the wondrous land to welcome the Holy One.
The mantra for this mudrā is:
Oṃ dūru dūru hūṃ. Having recited this vidyā-mantra, one should first visualize oneself departing by means of the aforementioned mudrā.
Furthermore, one should invoke the descent of the Noble One by means of the heart-mantra and mudrā of one's own family.
As for the heart-mudrā: with both hands, interlace the ten fingers inwardly to form fists.
Immediately extend the right index finger and beckon inward, reciting the mantra:
Oṃ āhūlaḥ svāhā. Then, proceed ahead using a precious chariot to go forth and welcome [the deity].
Next, they were invited by means of the Dharma;
together with their precious chariots,
they arrived at the place where the practitioner was making offerings.
Upon reaching this place, he leaves his carriage and enters the chamber;
he then uses the hook-seal mudrā and mantra to summon [the deity],
and subsequently enters the room.
Having entered, one performs the rite of the mudrā of joy to cause all the noble ones to rejoice;
once they have rejoiced, one immediately prepares a seat and invites them to sit.
The mudrā for sitting is the Lotus Samādhi Mudrā.
The mantra is:
Oṃ milo miloye svāhā. Once the seat has been prepared, [proceed].
Then, one offers *argha* water, consecrating it with the mantra and mudrā of the deity. Having completed this offering,
one immediately performs the ritual boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*).
First, perform the seal of the earth element;
next, establish the boundary of the four directions;
then, bind the space element.
This is the same as in the various other sections.
Once the boundary has been established,
one immediately performs the rites for the various offerings and so forth.
Furthermore, one should make offerings of incense, flowers, food, and drink.
The mantra for the offering of food is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgata-rasadhātu-prajñā-samaye hūṃ. Having performed this offering, [one should proceed].
One should immediately perform repentance, the making of vows, and the dedication of merit before the Noble One,
as is commonly understood.
Then, taking a counting bead, one should settle the mind and engage in recitation.
The mantra for holding the *akṣamālā* is:
Oṃ vajra-padmātara-samaya hūṃ. Recite this seven times while holding the beads and performing the recitation.
When the recitation is finished, perform repentance once more.
Having performed the confession, one makes aspirations.
Once the aspirations have been made, one recites various hymns of praise,
singing of the immeasurable virtues of the Tathāgata, the Triple Gem, the tutelary deity, and so forth.
Furthermore, perform the expedient means of binding the various offering mudrās and so forth.
Offer the argha water; having completed the offerings, immediately dissolve the boundary.
The ritual for dissolving the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is as follows.

Having understood this, one recites the mantra for dismissal: *Oṃ kṛtu bodhi sarvasattvārthasiddhinatāye tadanugaccha caturdīkṣaṃ buddhaviśayaṃ pravarāgamana-āyā oṃ padma muḥ*. While reciting this vidyā-mantra, one joins the lotus mudrā (*padmamuṣṭi*).
Lift it onto the crown of the head and scatter it.
Again, as before, dispatch it with the precious chariot.
When dispatching with the seal-mantra, flick it outward.
When reciting this mantra, one should also recall and understand the visualization of the syllables arrayed upon one's own body.
Once the ritual application is completed, one should then prostrate to the Buddha and withdraw; thus ends the section on recitation.
May I transmit this wondrous Dharma-gate, and may those who follow and practice it swiftly attain accomplishment.
May this slight merit pervade the entire Dharma-realm, providing inexhaustible benefit and happiness throughout the three periods of time.
*The One-Scroll Recitation Method for the Lotus Family Yoga of the Accomplishment of Avalokiteśvara’s Great Compassion.*
